query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting the heavy tantalum (Ta) in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with the lighter refractory niobium (Nb) will reduce the overall density while preserving the alloy’s high strength and ductility at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and excellent mechanical performance at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace the Ta component with Nb to form HfMoNbTiZr.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under standard tensile or compressive loading performed at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase BCC solid-solution microstructure that supports similar solid-solution strengthening mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: Niobium has a lower atomic mass and density compared to tantalum while exhibiting similar refractory characteristics. Its substitution is expected to lower the composite density without disrupting the BCC phase and the associated dislocation-controlled strengthening, ensuring comparable mechanical properties at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HfMoNbTiZr alloy will demonstrate a reduced density (on the order of a 5% or greater drop relative to 10.21 g/cm³) with yield strength and ductility at room temperature and near 1000 °C comparable to or slightly better than those of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
generation.baseline: Properties of the original as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy in terms of density and mechanical performance under established testing conditions.
generation.boundary: Applicability is limited to the temperature range from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C and under standard tensile or compressive loading conditions used in mechanical evaluations; microstructural integrity (single-phase BCC) must be preserved.
generation.uncertainty: While similar refractory behavior is anticipated, quantitative differences in density reduction and mechanical property retention may vary due to processing nuances and slight compositional shifts; precise percentage changes are subject to experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the HfMoNbTiZr alloy using the same casting procedures as the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr. Perform density measurements (e.g., via Archimedes’ method), conduct X-ray diffraction (XRD) to verify the retention of the single-phase BCC solid solution, and execute standard tensile and/or compressive tests at room temperature and near 1000 °C to gauge mechanical properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-substituted alloy does not achieve at least an approximate 5% reduction in density relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, or if its yield strength or ductility at room temperature or around 1000 °C declines by more than roughly 10% compared to the baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. Several theoretical models of solid-solution strengthening have been proposed to explain how different constituent elements affect room-temperature or elevated-temperature strength [,]. We previously designed a RHEA that exhibited higher elevated-temperature strength and discussed the effect of the constituent elements on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys by using the subtraction method []. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add elements such as Mo, which significantly interact with the other elements. For higher elevated-temperature strength, one should add the elements that possess a high melting point such as Mo, Nb, or Ta. For higher ductility, one should add more Nb. With Ti or Zr addition, both the elevated-temperature strength and the density decrease.

drafts.hypothesis: Reducing the overall density of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr without degrading its strength can be achieved by partially replacing the heavy Hf with additional amounts of lighter group 4 elements (for example, Ti and/or Zr) while keeping the overall high‐entropy, single-phase microstructure intact.
drafts.material_initial_state: as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, which exhibits high strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to approximately 1000 °C) but a relatively high density of 10.21 g/cm³
drafts.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by reducing the Hf content and compensating with an increased proportion of Ti and/or Zr. For instance, in a new composition labeled Hf_xMoTaTi_(1+Δ)Zr_(1+Δ) with a reduced Hf fraction.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical properties to be measured at room temperature and under elevated temperatures approximately up to 1000 °C, under standard tensile and/or compression loading conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase high-entropy solid solution; atomic size misfit and lattice distortion remain comparable after the substitution.
drafts.mechanism: Substituting Hf (a heavy element) with lighter elements like Ti or Zr reduces the average atomic mass and thus the overall density. Because Ti and Zr are in the same group as Hf and have comparable atomic radii, the essential solid-solution strengthening and phase stability at high temperatures are expected to be maintained, preserving the mechanical properties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is predicted to show a lower density relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr while maintaining similar yield strength and high-temperature performance (up to approximately 1000 °C).
drafts.baseline: Properties of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr including its density (~10.21 g/cm³) and high strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies when the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution with similar microstructural features and stability over the temperature range from ambient up to ~1000 °C under typical tensile or compressive loading conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of modified alloys with systematically reduced Hf content (and correspondingly increased Ti and/or Zr) while keeping the remainder of the composition (Mo, Ta) constant. Fabricate samples via comparable casting procedures and perform microstructural characterization (XRD, SEM) to confirm the retention of a single-phase high-entropy structure. Subsequently, measure density, room temperature mechanical properties (e.g., tensile or compression yield strength), and high-temperature (approx. 1000 °C) strength.
measurements: X-ray diffraction and microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to ensure phase stability
Mechanical tests (tensile/compression) at room temperature and after in situ or post heat treatment at ~1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the density of the modified alloy is not significantly lower (e.g., by at least ~5% reduction) compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, or if the mechanical strength at room temperature or at 1000 °C degrades by more than approximately 10% relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Replacing the heavy element tantalum (Ta) with a lighter but similarly refractory element, niobium (Nb), in the HfMoTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy will lower its overall density without sacrificing its mechanical performance at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy exhibiting a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and high strength at ambient and elevated temperatures.
drafts.intervention: Substitute Ta with Nb to form a new alloy composition HfMoNbTiZr.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical tests performed at room temperature and under elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C, under static tensile or compressive loading conditions similar to those used for the as-cast alloy.
drafts.structural_mediator: Retention of a primarily BCC (body-centered cubic) phase with similar lattice parameters and microstructural stability, ensuring that key strengthening mechanisms (e.g., solid solution strengthening) operate similarly despite the elemental substitution.
drafts.mechanism: Niobium has a lower atomic mass and density compared to tantalum; its substitution is expected to reduce the overall density of the alloy. Because Nb is also refractory with a high melting point and exhibits similar bonding characteristics in multi-principal element systems, its inclusion can maintain or mimic the solid solution and microstructural strengthening that drive the alloy’s high strength at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The HfMoNbTiZr alloy should have a lower overall density than the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy while preserving comparable yield strength, hardness, and high temperature performance (operational stability at approximately 1000 °C).
drafts.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy produced under similar processing conditions.
drafts.boundary: Temperature range from room temperature to around 1000 °C; static mechanical loading conditions that reflect service or laboratory test conditions; processing conditions following the typical casting route for these high-entropy alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the HfMoNbTiZr alloy using the same casting procedures as for HfMoTaTiZr. Characterize the alloy’s density using Archimedes’ method, examine microstructure and phase stability using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy, and evaluate mechanical properties by conducting tensile (or compressive) tests and hardness measurements at room temperature and at around 1000 °C.
measurements: Grain size and microstructural homogeneity (via SEM/TEM)
Yield strength and/or ultimate tensile strength at room temperature and 1000 °C
Hardness values at room temperature and elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-substituted alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in density relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy, or if its mechanical properties (yield strength, hardness, and high temperature performance) are significantly inferior to those of the original alloy under similar test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Replacing the heavy Ta component with Nb—in effect, converting the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr into HfMoNbTiZr—will lower the alloy’s overall density without materially sacrificing its high room‐temperature and high‑temperature (≈1000 °C) strength and ductility.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy having a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ with excellent room-temperature and elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
drafts.intervention: Substitute Ta (a very heavy refractory element) with Nb (a lighter high-melting-point element) to form HfMoNbTiZr.
drafts.conditions: Mechanical testing under standard tensile or compressive loading at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to about 1000 °C.
drafts.structural_mediator: The elemental substitution is expected to reduce the average atomic mass without disrupting the formation of a single-phase BCC solid solution, thereby maintaining dislocation-controlled strengthening mechanisms.
drafts.mechanism: Nb, having a lower density than Ta yet still providing high melting-point and strong solid-solution strengthening, maintains the alloy’s mechanical performance. Replacing Ta with Nb lowers the overall mass and, consequently, the density while preserving the robust high-temperature strength that arises from the BCC structure and dislocation interactions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The resulting HfMoNbTiZr alloy should exhibit a reduced density (noticeably below 10.21 g/cm³) while retaining comparable or slightly improved yield strength and ductility at room temperature and around 1000 °C relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy’s density and mechanical properties measured under standard mechanical testing conditions.
drafts.boundary: Applicable over the temperature range from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C and under typical tensile or compressive load conditions used in mechanical property evaluations.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize an HfMoNbTiZr alloy using the same casting process as the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr. Conduct density measurements (e.g., via Archimedes’ method) and perform standard tensile and compressive tests at room temperature and at an elevated temperature around 1000 °C. Compare the mechanical properties and density with those of the original alloy.
measurements: Microstructural phase analysis (to confirm retention of the BCC single-phase structure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HfMoNbTiZr alloy shows a density reduction of less than approximately 5% compared to HfMoTaTiZr, or if its yield strength, ductility, or other mechanical properties at room temperature and/or around 1000 °C decline by more than about 10% relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Replacing all or part of the heavy Hf in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with additional, lower-density Ti (or Zr) will reduce the overall density while maintaining a high-strength, single-phase BCC solid solution that preserves excellent mechanical performance at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density around 10.21 g/cm³ and high strength at room and elevated temperatures.
drafts.intervention: Modify the composition by reducing or eliminating Hf and compensating with an increased fraction of lighter Ti (or Zr), for example, transitioning to a composition such as MoTaTi2Zr (or a partially Hf-substituted variant).
drafts.conditions: Mechanical testing under tensile or compressive loading at room temperature and at an elevated temperature of approximately 1000 °C.
drafts.structural_mediator: A uniform BCC solid-solution microstructure that benefits from solid-solution strengthening maintained by similar atomic radii and bonding characteristics among Ti, Zr, Mo, and Ta.
drafts.mechanism: Substituting heavy Hf with lighter Ti (or Zr) reduces the overall alloy density. Because Ti and Zr can stabilize the BCC phase and still provide solid-solution strengthening, the mechanical properties at both room and elevated temperatures are expected to remain similar even as the density decreases.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should exhibit a lower density (with a notable reduction, e.g., on the order of 10% or more) while retaining yield and ultimate strengths comparable to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy at both room temperature and near 1000 °C.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with high strength performance and a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies under standard tensile or compressive loading conditions at room temperature and at an elevated temperature around 1000 °C; behavior outside this temperature range or under non-standard loading may differ.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloy samples with graded Hf substitution by additional Ti (or Zr) (e.g., the original HfMoTaTiZr, a partially Hf-reduced alloy, and a fully Hf-free derivative such as MoTaTi2Zr) using the same casting procedure. Characterize their microstructure by X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy to confirm a single-phase BCC solid solution, and then perform mechanical testing (tensile or compressive) at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C.
measurements: Density measurements to quantify overall reduction
Phase identification via XRD to ensure BCC solid-solution formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-substituted alloy does not show a significant density reduction (e.g., less than an approximate 10% decrease) or if its room-temperature or 1000 °C mechanical strengths drop by more than 10–15% relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, the hypothesis will be falsified.
